   - Detailed description of the chosen/best idea, including rationale, pseudocode, and implementation notes

The report must be focused, technically accurate. Being concise with 200-500 words without trivial and redundant information.
Support all claims with evidence and references, and remain tightly aligned with the target problem.

## Current Code Workflow (from code analyzer)
# Model Overview (for Diagnosis)

The supplied code diagnoses item embedding geometry and positive-versus-negative score separation. Model internals are not provided: sequence representations come from `log2feats(sequence)`, and `predict_score(features, items)` produces logits. The probe evaluates every valid sequence position; it does not explicitly extract a final user representation.

# Diagnosis Inputs & Hooks

`DiagnosisProbe(view, device)` stores the compatibility view, accessing `item_emb`, `log2feats`, `predict_score`, `meta_data`, `review_data`, and `user_train`. The latter two are stored but unused.

The loader supplies `(None, sequence, positive, negative)` tensors of shape B × L. Sequences are converted to NumPy before feature extraction. Positive and negative IDs are stacked into B × L × 2 for scoring. Positions with positive ID zero are excluded.

# Probes & Metrics

- **`embedding_collapse_score`**: Samples up to 2,048 nonpadding item embeddings with seed 42, normalizes them, averages off-diagonal pairwise cosine similarities, and maps the result to [0,1]. Higher values indicate greater directional alignment; approximately 0.5 corresponds to mean cosine zero. This is a geometric proxy, not recommendation diversity.
- **`pos_neg_margin_mean` / `pos_neg_margin_p10`**: Mean and lower tenth percentile of positive-minus-negative logits across at most ten training batches. Larger values indicate stronger separation.
- **`pos_neg_neg_beats_pos_rate`**: Fraction of margins below zero; lower is better.
- **`pos_neg_small_margin_rate`**: Fraction below 0.5; lower indicates fewer weakly separated pairs.
- **`pos_neg_margin_category_breakdown`**: Counts low-margin and wrong-ranking positions and their positive/negative item categories. Categories are unavailable in this task, so category lists should remain empty.

# Perturbation & Tests

No sequence shuffling, input perturbation, sensitivity testing, or SVD is performed. Margin scoring uses evaluation mode without gradients. The probe does not restore the previous training mode.

# MODEL_DIAGNOSIS Schema & Limitations

`run_full_diagnosis` returns `metrics` and `metric_definitions`. `diagnosis_interpreter_prompt` embeds both into a prompt requesting JSON with `status`, `core_findings`, `key_implications`, and `evidence`; it does not itself generate that interpretation.

These probes measure sampled training separation and embedding alignment, not validation HR@10, generalization, calibration, or simulator traits. Margin magnitudes depend on logit scale and sampled negatives. Empty valid-position samples return zero margin statistics, which must not be interpreted as healthy performance.

Thus, HR@10 against 99 negatives and full-catalog HR@10 measure different ranking challenges. No located evidence establishes diagnostic probes as reliable predictors of gains across these exact four Amazon datasets.

Practical implication: use scale-invariant probes—positive-item rank percentile, pairwise win rate, and Kendall/Spearman agreement across identical candidate sets—rather than raw score margins. Quantify sampled/full-catalog disagreement using validation-target hit-status disagreement, target-rank percentiles, and model-order reversals across trials. Comparing top-10 lists drawn from different candidate universes directly confounds candidate availability with ranking quality. Fixed validation users and negative candidates support paired comparisons, but sampled HR@10 can reverse full-catalog model rankings, even in expectation; interpret results strictly under the pinned benchmark ([Krichene–Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Recommended comparison: retain each user’s binary hit for both models; bootstrap users within each category, using identical resampled indices for both models, then average the four category differences. Report the macro difference, interval, and category results. This estimates user-sampling uncertainty conditional on fitted models and fixed candidates; it excludes training randomness and candidate-sampling variability. Paired resampling has precedent in retrieval evaluation ([Smucker et al.](https://ciir-publications.cs.umass.edu/getpdf.php?id=744)). With 200 users/category, one changed hit shifts category HR by 0.005 and macro HR by 0.00125.

Adaptive validation overfitting is a separate issue: selecting hyperparameters and checkpoints from repeated validation feedback creates selection optimism; an ordinary bootstrap of the selected winner does not remove it ([Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html), [Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629)). Practical synthesis for the 43,200 GPU-second budget: predeclare a small hypothesis-driven search, checkpoint evaluation schedule, stopping rules, and deterministic tie-breaking; count every checkpoint comparison and charge failed runs to the budget. Use predetermined successive-halving rungs to concentrate compute, while allowing sufficient training before pruning ([Hyperband](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v18/16-558.html)). Preserve seeds 0/42, all categories, splits, and candidate sets. Log every attempted configuration and its cost; report intervals as exploratory comparison evidence, not selection-corrected guarantees. Freeze the configuration and checkpoint before the host’s independent held-out evaluation; access no test labels during search.

Closest match: Petrov et al., [Do Sequential Recommendation Benchmarks Really Require Higher-Order Sequence Modelling?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19833) (2026), compares last-item Markov/factorized controls with recency-weighted pairwise history models, SeqRules and PCTM, and SASRec/eSASRec. PCTM uses transition counts, exponential or head–tail history weighting, smoothing, and popularity correction; no content features. Pairwise probes outperform reproduced Transformers on four of five datasets, while ML-20M retains a Transformer advantage. Crucial distinction: order-sensitive pairwise transitions do not establish higher-order sequence reasoning. The study does not fully isolate each weighting/smoothing component; its full-catalogue NDCG results cannot be transferred directly to this sampled HR@10 benchmark.

Klenitskiy et al., [Does It Look Sequential?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008), tests original versus shuffled histories to assess order dependence. [HAM](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10034966/) supplies complementary interaction-only controls: mean/max pooling over recent windows, with ablations of short-history associations and persistent user preferences; mean pooling consistently beats max pooling in its experiments. [RSS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643) emphasizes recent interactions through training-example sampling, so its improvements concern the training distribution rather than isolating inference-time exponential pooling.

Suggested matched ablation, synthesized from these studies: last-item embedding alone; uniform pooling over the same recent window; exponential pooling with identical embeddings and objective; each pooling variant plus a separately ablated last-item residual; then SASRec. Hold loss, negatives, embedding size, history window, and tuning budget fixed. Shuffle older history while preserving the last item to probe additional order dependence. These controls distinguish history membership, recency weighting, immediate transitions, and contextual sequence modeling; none of the cited results alone establishes the proposed residual’s contribution.
